projects.title: DoorDash wage theft settlement built on a data investigation
projects.description: The Mamdani administration's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection announced a $131.5 million settlement with DoorDash on September 22, 2026, the largest municipal wage theft recovery in the city's history. Investigators built the case by analyzing more than 152 million individual payment transactions and 110 million working hours from DoorDash's own records, most of the recovery tied to how the company calculated pay for time Dashers spend online between deliveries.
projects.why_interesting: A regulator using a company's own transaction-level data at this scale, rather than worker complaints or spot audits, to build a nine-figure enforcement case.

projects.title: September 11th Document Portal
projects.description: The Mamdani administration opened a searchable public portal at nyc.gov/sept11docs on September 8, 2026, with an initial release of about 170,000 pages of city records on health concerns, air quality, and the city's response to the World Trade Center attacks, days ahead of the 25th anniversary. The release settled a long-running public-records dispute and includes internal correspondence showing officials had doubts about air-quality assurances before making them publicly.
projects.why_interesting: A quarter-century of internal city records made keyword-searchable in one release, rather than trickling out through individual FOIL requests. Slightly outside this week's window but never previously surfaced in this scan.

projects.title: Mapping New York's contaminated water systems
projects.description: New York Focus and NYCity News Service analyzed 2024 state Department of Health testing data and found 79 public water systems across New York, serving roughly 575,000 people, with contamination exceeding state limits for PFAS and other toxins. Published September 8, 2026.
projects.why_interesting: Turns routine, system-by-system state water-testing filings into a single statewide count of who is actually exposed, rather than one contaminated town at a time.

projects.title: Toronto's AI chatbot for 311 services
projects.description: Toronto is rolling out an AI chatbot on a redesigned 311 website, reported by CBC News in September 2026, to handle general inquiries such as pothole-repair timelines while human agents keep answering phones for complex cases. The new site adds mobile-first design, improved search, and simplified categories so residents do not need to know city-department jargon to route a request. Full launch is planned by the end of 2026.
projects.why_interesting: A concrete test of whether an AI layer over 311 request data actually reduces the friction of filing a complaint, rather than just moving the same categories online.

projects.title: DataDiver adds a restaurant-inspections view
projects.description: DataDiver, an open-source civic data platform built on San Francisco's public Socrata feeds, recently shipped a restaurant-inspections view telling the story through turnover, closures, and ownership changes rather than a raw inspection list, alongside filterable traffic-safety stat cards and an updated geographic navigator. Code is MIT licensed; editorial content and derived datasets are CC BY 4.0.
projects.why_interesting: A volunteer-built alternative to a city's own open-data portal, adding narrative framing that the raw Socrata feed does not provide on its own.

projects.title: Block and Paper: every building, by year built
projects.description: An interactive map plotting building construction years across cities worldwide, including New York, covering 1800 to 2026 with about 90 percent of 1.67 million building footprints matched to a recorded year. Zoomed out, it draws 100-meter cells colored by median building age; zoomed in, individual footprints and years appear. A height mode switches the color scale to show a city's skyline relief instead of age. Featured in AnyChart's DataViz Weekly roundup on September 18, 2026.
projects.why_interesting: Turns building-age records that most cities publish separately into one comparable layer, so a neighborhood's construction era reads at a glance instead of a lot-by-lot lookup.

projects.title: SeasonMap: when to travel where, by the weather
projects.description: A world map scoring roughly 1,400 destinations on how their weather feels for a given month and trip style (city walking, beach, hiking, snow), built from ten years of climate normals corrected against nearby weather stations, plus layers for crowd levels, local events, and hazards. Shared on Hacker News and featured in AnyChart's DataViz Weekly roundup in September 2026.
projects.why_interesting: An independent project turning a subjective travel-planning question into a proper comfort-score dataset across many places at once, a useful model for scoring conditions rather than just mapping raw numbers.
